ゆめ が かないます ように — May the dream come true

You learn ～ように (“so that”, especially after the potential and the negative), ～ように する / ～ように して いる (“I make sure to”, “I make a habit of”) and ～ように いう / たのむ (“he told me to / she asked me to”), plus the first kanji of N3; Ioana reveals to Mihai and Ana a secret she has kept for a whole year: she has won a one-year scholarship to a university in Kyoto.
to come true (a dream, a wish)
to get used to (something: ～に なれる)
to hold back, to be shy (about asking)
I’ll write it down in advance so I don’t forget.
I practise every day so that I can speak Japanese.
I make sure to go to bed early every day.
My mother told me to write an e-mail every week.
To say “so that” with ～ように after potential verbs (はなせる ように), negatives (わすれない ように) and non-volitional verbs (なる, わかる, みえる), and to know when to stick with ～ために (ch. 44).
To say “I make sure to / I try to” with ～ように する and “I make a habit of” with ～ように して いる, and to tell them apart from ～ように なる and ～こと に する.
To report what someone told you or asked you to do with ～ように いう / たのむ / つたえる / ちゅうい する (also in the passive: ～ように いわれた).
To use ～ように at the end of a sentence: as a short reminder (わすれない ように) and as a wish (ごうかく できます ように).
To read the first kanji of N3: 一, 年, 大, 学, 生, 今 (and to review 日, 本, 月, 十, 人).

A Saturday in early September, in the afternoon, in the flat in Cotroceni. It’s the usual time for Japanese practice with Ioana. Rosa Elena (1 year and almost 8 months) is playing on the rug with Sakura’s little drum. Ioana comes in with an envelope in her hand and flushed cheeks.
Hello. Today I came because I have something important to tell you.
What happened? You’re red as a beetroot. Sit down first.
(Taking out the envelope) Actually… I’m going to be able to study for a year at a university in Japan! I managed to get a scholarship.
In Kyoto. From October, for one year, I’ll study at a university in Kyoto.
Kyoto! But that’s Mrs Fumiko’s city! Congratulations, Ioana!
But when did you take the exam? I had no idea.
From winter to spring I had an exam and an interview at the embassy. I’d have been ashamed if I failed, so I made sure not to tell anyone.
Ah! So back in spring, when you said you had “a job interview” and we practised so much keigo…
Yes, that was what it was for. I asked you to help me so that I could speak properly at the interview. I’m sorry I kept it a secret.
(Laughing) Don’t apologise. If my keigo was of any use to you, I’m happy.
Have you told Mrs Fumiko yet?
I sent her an e-mail yesterday. And this morning the reply came… she asked me to come and help at the teahouse at weekends!
Mrs Fumiko is so kind. I bet she also wrote “don’t hold back”, didn’t she?
Yes, that’s exactly what it said! And she says she’ll teach me every week, so that I can learn how to make tea.
How wonderful! But alone, abroad for the first time… aren’t you anxious?
A little. That’s why, so that I can get used to life in Japan quickly, I’m already making sure to listen to Japanese news every day.
As a doctor, just one thing. Winter in Kyoto is cold, so be careful not to catch a cold. And make sure you sleep properly at night.
(Laughing) Yes, doctor. My mother said the same thing. To eat properly every day.
(Picking up Rosa Elena) Look, Rosa Elena. Ioana is going to Japan.
(Rosa Elena grabs her finger) Oh, is she telling me “don’t go”?
She doesn’t talk yet, but I’m sure she understands.
So that Rosa Elena doesn’t forget me, I’ll video call every week.
Right. Then today’s practice topic will be “So you don’t get stuck in Kyoto”!

“koto ni narimashita” = it has been decided that; thing
so that; “~yō ni suru” = to make sure to; “~yō ni iu / tanomu” = to tell / ask (someone) to
“tetsudai ni kuru” = to come and help

doctor (as a form of address); teacher
so you don’t have problems, so you don’t get stuck

shō-ga-ku-ki-n: the “o” in しょう is long (sho-o), and the “u” in “ku” is barely heard between the two “k” sounds: “shōgak(u)kin”. ryū-ga-ku: りゅ is a single syllable — not “ri-u”; the Japanese “r” is a light tap, almost like an “l” (or the “tt” in American “butter”), then a long “u”.
ta-i-shi-ka-n: the “i” in “shi” sits between “sh” and “k” (both voiceless), so it almost disappears: “taish’kan”. me-n-se-tsu: ん is a full beat, and the “u” of つ at the end is very weak: “mensets’”.

yo-o-ni: long “o” (よう = yo-o), then “ni” joined on. Don’t say a short “yoni” and don’t pause between よう and に: in speech it sounds like one word. At the end of a wish (かないます ように) the voice falls gently.
1. ～ように: “so that” (a goal you can’t control directly)

In ch. 44 you learned ～ために: “so that / in order to”, after a VOLITIONAL verb, with the same subject (べんきょう する ために いく). Now comes its sibling, ～ように, which you already glimpsed in explanation 5 of ch. 44. It also translates as “so that”, but it goes after things you can’t do directly by willpower: being ABLE to do something (potential), NOT doing something (negative), becoming, understanding, seeing, hearing — or when SOMEONE ELSE reaches the goal.
I practised so that I could speak at the interview.
I write it down so I don’t forget.
I sit at the front so that I can see well.
X が + verb + ように
I write big so that the children can read it.
The verb before ように is always in the dictionary form or the ～ない form — never in the past and never in ～ます (with a single exception: the wish ～ます ように, in explanation 3).
The potential does NOT go with ために: ✗ はなせる ために → ✓ はなせる ように. The negative doesn’t really either (～ない ために is stiff, written style): for “so as not to” almost always say ～ない ように.

In English you just say “so that” or “in order to” everywhere. Trick: ask yourself “can I do this by my own will, right now?”. “To go” — yes → ために. “To be able to speak”, “not to forget”, “for it to be seen” — doesn’t depend only on me → ように.
2. ～ように する / ～ように して いる: “I make sure to”, “I make a habit of”
Put する after ように and you get an effort: “I act so that…”, “I make sure to…”. With ～て いる it becomes a habit kept up on purpose: “for a while now, I’ve always been trying to…”.
I make sure (I’ve made it a habit) to listen to Japanese news every day.
I was making sure not to tell anyone.
From now on I’ll make sure to go to bed early.
I try not to eat too many sweets.
Three expressions that look alike but say different things. You’ve met them all:
change: I’ve COME to (be able to / do)
effort: I make SURE to, I try to

～こと に した = “I decided” (one moment, a clear decision). ～ように して いる = “I try to” (softer, you don’t promise you always succeed). Japanese people often use ように して いる when talking about health or habits, precisely because it sounds modest.
3. ～ように いう / たのむ: “he told me to…”, “she asked me to…” (and ～ように! at the end)

When you report what someone asked of you, you don’t have to quote their exact words. You put the verb in the dictionary form or ～ない + ように + a verb of speaking: いう (to say), たのむ (to ask), つたえる (to pass on), ちゅうい する (to warn), かく (to write).
My mother told me to eat properly.
Mrs Fumiko asked me to come and help.
Mihai warned me not to catch a cold.
Ioana told Mrs Fumiko not to put it in her tea.

You’ll often hear them in the PASSIVE (ch. 31), from the point of view of the person receiving the request: はは に たべる ように いわれた (my mother told me to…), ふみこさん に くる ように たのまれた (I was asked by Mrs Fumiko to…). The person asking takes に.
Don’t put ～て ください before ように: ✗ きて ください ように いった → ✓ くる ように いった. ～て ください only goes in a direct quote: 「きて ください」 と いった.
At the end of a sentence, ように has two more uses:
よる は ちゃんと ねる ように。 (Make sure you sleep properly at night.)

You’ll see the form ～ます ように written on the wooden plaques (えま) at Japanese shrines and on the paper strips of the たなばた festival: “May I pass the exam”, “May my family be healthy”. It’s the only place where ます comes before ように.
4. Comparison: ために or ように?
Both mean “so that”, but they pick different verbs. Look at the pairs below one by one:
volitional: いく, かう, べんきょう する
non-volitional: potential, ～ない, なる, わかる, みえる
can be the same or different
yes: けんこう の ために (for your health)
no (✗ けんこう の ように in the sense of “so that”)
I applied for the scholarship IN ORDER TO study abroad.
I studied every evening SO THAT I COULD study abroad.
I’m saving money to go to Japan. (go = volition → ために)
I’m saving money so that I can go to Japan. (can = potential → ように)
I spoke loudly so that everyone could hear. (きこえる = non-volitional)

Careful, よう has other lives too: いつも の ように (as usual), おなじ ように (in the same way) — here よう means “way, manner”, not purpose. You’ll see them in detail in ch. 66. They’re easy to spot: before よう comes の or おなじ, not a verb.

Ioana has won a scholarship offered by the Japanese government (にほん せいふ の しょうがくきん) to students who study Japanese at university. It is awarded through the Japanese embassy in each country, and the selection usually has several stages: the application, a written test (Japanese) and an interview. The scholarship for Japanese-studies students lasts about a year and usually starts in autumn, around October. The exact conditions change from year to year, so always check with the embassy.

At an interview in Japan (めんせつ) basic keigo and the way you walk in matter a lot: you knock three times, say しつれい します, and wait to be told どうぞ、おかけ ください before you sit down. Ioana practised all this with Mihai without telling him why.
6. Kanji: 一 年 大 学 生 今

From N3 on, we start writing a few kanji in the texts, little by little. In each chapter you learn a few new ones; the rest stays in kana, and the spaces between words stay. Each kanji usually has a Chinese reading (音読み, おんよみ, used mostly in compound words) and a Japanese reading (訓読み, くんよみ, used mostly on its own or with kana endings).
Review from earlier chapters: 日 (に / ひ) and 本 (ほん) → 日本 (にほん, Japan); 月 (がつ / つき) and 十 → 十月 (じゅうがつ, October); 人 (じん / ひと) → 日本人 (にほんじん, Japanese person).
Some words have “special” readings that can’t be worked out from the kanji: 今年 is read ことし (this year), 今日 is read きょう (today), 一人 is read ひとり. That’s why, for now, we still write them in kana.

Don’t be scared of multiple readings: choose by the neighbours. A kanji next to another kanji → usually the Chinese reading (大学 = だいがく). A kanji followed by kana → usually the Japanese one (大きい = おおきい).

ふみこさん の へんじ — Mrs Fumiko’s reply
The e-mail Ioana received on the morning of the dialogue. Mrs Fumiko writes politely, with keigo (ch. 36–38). Look for her requests: how do they become “～ように たのまれました” when Ioana tells them?
Dear Ioana, thank you for the wonderful news.
When I heard you are coming to Kyoto in October, my sister in Madrid and I were overjoyed together on the phone.
If it suits you, would you be so kind as to come and help me at the teahouse at weekends?
I am getting on in years myself, so having a young person by my side would be a great help.
And so that you can learn little by little how to make tea, let us practise together.
I have just one request: please, whatever you do, don’t hold back.
And please give my regards to Mrs Doina in Bucharest. I cannot forget the taste of that cherry jam.
I look forward to seeing you in Kyoto. Fumiko

ひみつ の めんせつ — The secret interview
In August, Mihai, Ana and Rosa Elena went to the village again. To give Grandpa the printed photo of the spoon that Sakura had taken in Kyoto.
Grandpa looked at the photo for a long time, then carefully put it in a place of honour, next to the photograph of the two soldiers.
“Here I can see it every day. And so that Vasile and Ileana can see it well too.”
Rosa Elena sat down on the little stool with the rose and patted Grandpa gently on the knee.
“Well, look at that, she can already sit by herself.” Grandpa, pleased, stroked Rosa Elena’s head.
“So that the little one doesn’t forget the village, come every summer,” said Grandpa.
September came, and the students returned to the university in Bucharest.
On the evening of the Saturday when she had revealed her secret to Mihai and Ana, on her way back to the dorm, Ioana was remembering the past year.
Last December, a poster had been put up on the university notice board.
“Japanese Government Scholarship. You can study for one year at a university in Japan.”
Her heart started pounding. But straight away she got scared. If she failed, she might disappoint everyone.
So Ioana made sure not to tell anyone. Not her roommate in the dorm, not her parents in Iași, not Mihai and Ana.
Her roommate wondered: “What are you doing up so late at night these days?”, but Ioana only answered: “A paper.”
Every evening, after her university classes, she studied kanji and grammar so that she would pass the exam. And she washed her face with cold water so that she wouldn’t get sleepy.
In January the written test took place at the embassy. Next came the interview.
She wanted to be able to use keigo properly at the interview. But she couldn’t practise alone.
So, at the Saturday practice, she asked Mihai: “I have a job interview.”
Without asking anything, Mihai played the role of the interviewer. From knocking on the door to how to bow.
The day of the interview, in March. In a large room sat three interviewers.
Ioana knocked on the door three times, said “Excuse me” and only then went in. Exactly as she had practised with Mihai.
The questions were hard, but the keigo came out so naturally that even she was surprised.
At the very end she was asked: “Why do you want to go to Japan?”
Ioana thought for a moment, then told the story of the wallet found on the tram.
“In the wallet there was a photo with something written in hiragana on the back. That photo is where my Japan began.”
“And I promised a Japanese lady who has a teahouse in Kyoto: ‘I will come without fail.’ I want to go so that I can keep my promise.”
One of the interviewers gave a broad smile.
In April, around the time Mihai and Ana came back from Kyoto, the first result arrived: “You have been recommended.”
But whether she could really go was still unknown. She waited a long time again, until the university in Japan was decided.
And this week, at last, the e-mail came: “It’s settled: a university in Kyoto. One year, from October.”
“Kyoto… Mrs Fumiko’s city.” Alone in her dorm room, Ioana sobbed out loud.
That evening, Ioana phoned her parents in Iași. When her mother heard the news, she got a lump in her throat and burst into tears.
“Why didn’t you tell us sooner?” “I thought that if I failed, I’d disappoint you…”
Her father was quiet, as usual. He said only this: “Make sure you don’t catch a cold over there. Take your thick coat.”
Before hanging up, her mother whispered: “Your father is crying right now next to me, you know.”
Her mother wiped her tears and told her to write an e-mail every week. “Before you leave, come home once. I’ll teach you how Grandma makes ciorbă (sour soup). So that you can make it in Japan too.”
The next day, Ioana went to talk to her teacher at the university. It was settled that she would interrupt her studies in Bucharest for a year.
Her teacher smiled: “Meet as many people as you can in Japan. And when you come back, tell everyone about it.”
The following Saturday, when Ioana came to Mihai’s, she met Mrs Doina on the stairs.
When she heard the news, Mrs Doina went straight back into her flat and brought three jars of cherry jam.
“One is yours. One is for Mrs Fumiko. And open the other one when you feel homesick.”
“And tell Mrs Fumiko not to put it in her tea. You spread it on bread!” Ioana laughed: “Yes, I’ll be sure to tell her.”
The topic of that day’s practice was tea. Ana took out the card she had got from Mrs Fumiko: “How to make good green tea”.
Ioana let the water cool a little and poured slowly. Carefully, down to the last drop.
“I want to practise many times beforehand, so that I don’t mess up in front of Mrs Fumiko.”
Rosa Elena reached for the teacup. When Ana said “No, it’s hot”, Rosa Elena pouted, just like in Kyoto.
Mihai was writing something at the table. What came out was a small card.
“I made myself a card too when Director Tanaka came, remember? This one is so you won’t have problems in Kyoto.”
On the card were written the address of Mrs Fumiko’s teahouse and words to use at the hospital: “I have a fever”, “It hurts here”.
“The best thing is not to get ill, but if you do, it’s so that you can explain properly.”
That day, just when Ioana was there, Sakura video called. Ever since Ana had shared the news in the group, she had been dying to talk to Ioana.
“Ioana, congratulations! But that’s not fair! I want to live in Kyoto too!”
Haruka said, laughing: “Sakura says you must come to Hiroshima too.”
“I’ll make you okonomiyaki!” Sakura made a circle with her fingers in front of the camera.
Ioana laughed and made a circle with her fingers too. “It’s a promise, then!”
Before leaving, Ioana crouched down in front of Rosa Elena. Rosa Elena squeezed her finger tight, as usual.
“Rosa Elena, your big sis is going to Japan for just one year. Don’t forget me, OK?”
Ioana hooked her little finger around the tiny one. “Pinky promise.”
Rosa Elena babbled something, but it wasn’t words yet. Still, she gazed at Ioana’s face and gave a broad smile.
“What she just said was surely ‘Have a good trip and come back safely’,” said Ana.
The departure was set for the last Saturday in September. Three weeks were left.
That night, Ioana looked up at the sky from the dorm window. Far away to the east, under the same sky, was Kyoto.
“May my dream come true,” whispered Ioana.

Listen to the dialogue 3 times. Note down every ように and put a letter next to it: P (purpose), E (effort, ように する / して いる), R (request, ように いう / たのむ) or F (at the end: reminder or wish).
Turn into indirect speech: 「まいにち れんしゅう して ください。」 → せんせい は まいにち れんしゅう する ように いいました。 Do the same with: 「おそく ならないで。」, 「てつだい に きて ください。」, 「しずか に して。」.

Role play: you are Ioana and you tell a friend (who plays Mihai) that you’re leaving for Kyoto. He gives you three pieces of advice with ～ない ように and ～ように して ね; you tell him what your parents told you (～ように いわれた).
